messages.mes:
The road took him with the morning traffic. Carts and a string of pack mules rolled toward the same gates, and a woman driving geese walked them along the ditch until the wall rose up close enough to shade the grass. The stone was old and patched in places, wide enough for two wagons abreast, and the gate stood open under a banner he didn't recognize. A bored guard watched the carts pass and gave Alaric the same half-glance he gave everyone else on foot.

Inside, Glassmere smelled of bread ovens and river water. The street sloped gently down from the gate between timber-fronted houses, three stories in some places, laundry strung between upper windows. A boy swept a step. Somewhere to the left a hammer rang on an anvil, steady as a clock. Two young people in matching grey satchels hurried past arguing about an examination, one of them gesturing with a rolled diagram, and a painted board in a shop window offered rune-work by the letter, prices listed beneath in neat columns.

He read signs as he went. The language sat in his head as if he'd always had it. Twice he took a wrong turning into a square with a fountain and a fish stall, and twice the street signs put him right again, until a wider road opened onto a small square of cobbles and a long, solid building with a deep porch.

The sign above its doors showed a shield crossed by a sword and a staff, painted fresh over older layers. Through the open doors came lamplight, the smell of ink and old leather, and the low noise of people with business of their own. Inside the hall, a long counter ran along the left wall, and a pair of adventurers stood at its far end, one of them tapping the counter while a clerk wrote. Benches lined the right wall. Papers were pinned in rows on a broad board at the back.

The morning let him stand there a moment, unnoticed.

The clerk at the near end of the counter looked up from a ledger. She was somewhere past forty, grey streaking brown hair pinned back tight, ink stains on the pads of her fingers. Behind her, shelves of bound rolls ran the length of the wall, each spine dated.

"Registration, is it." She pulled a fresh form toward her and dipped her pen. "Name?"

He gave it, and she wrote it out letter by letter, checking the spelling aloud. "Alaric. Fine. Now the part that costs you: the one-time fee is two silver. That covers your measuring, your slip, your listing in the rolls, and your Guild mark. It doesn't buy you anything else—no equipment, no favors, and it doesn't come back if you quit."

She set the pen down and looked at him properly for the first time, gaze flicking over the staff slung at his side and back to his face.

"Standard practice, so you hear it from the start: what you pay for here is membership. Guild Rank—Novice, for you, at the bottom like everyone else. That's our word for how much the Guild trusts you with contracts. Your Power Rank is a different thing entirely. We'll read it off the measuring stone, and it's yours whether you join or not. F is the floor. People climb it by getting stronger, not by paying us."

From under the counter she lifted a flat slate the size of a baking tray, its surface engraved with fine concentric lines, and set it on the counter with both hands.

"Hand goes on the stone, it reads what you are, and we write it down honestly. The rolls don't flatter anybody." She nudged the slate an inch toward him. "Two silver, then the stone. Whenever you're ready."

Two silver crossed the counter. The clerk counted them against the wood with her thumb, swept them into a locked drawer, and pulled the roll she'd started back in front of her.

"Hand flat on the stone. Fingers apart, don't press."

The slate's center held a crystal the size of a plum, set into the innermost ring of the engraving. When his palm settled over it the crystal warmed under his skin, and a pale light crept outward along the carved lines, ring by ring, until the outermost band held a faint steady glow. She leaned down to read it, lips moving slightly.

"F." She wrote it into the roll beside his name, no ceremony in it. "Power Rank F, Guild Rank Novice. That's the starting line for nearly everybody. The stone doesn't flatter and it doesn't lie, which is more than I can say for some of the people who stand where you're standing."

From a shallow tray under the counter she took a slim plate of dull bronze, the Guild's mark—shield, sword, staff—struck into the face. She inked his name beneath the stamp, rank below that, and pressed a strip of paper over it to blot.

"Your plate. It carries your listing, so any branch in the kingdoms can read who you are and where you stand with us. Don't lose it; replacing one costs more than joining did." She held it out across the counter, then dipped her pen again and turned a page. "Contracts are the board at the back. The ones marked F are what the Guild hands a Novice. You take one here at the desk, not off the wall—read it first, all of it. Most people who skip that part come back to pay for it."

messages.mes:
The stocky man was still counting out words with the clerk when Alaric set the beetle notice on the counter behind his elbow. She finished the other pair first—logged the wool cart, took their mark, sent them off with a jerk of her chin—then turned the notice around and read it as if she hadn't written half the ones on the board herself.

"Glimmerdeep." She pulled the contract roll toward her and copied the entry into it in a quick, slanted hand. "Academy's cleft. North of the city a morning's walk, up the valley where the stream comes out of the rock. You'll know the crystal by the glitter even before you're inside."

She took a slip from a flat drawer—stiff paper, the Guild's shield-and-staff seal at the foot—and pressed her stamp into it. The ink settled with a faint shimmer, the enchantment taking hold.

"You're on the roll for it as of now. That slip is your proof. When the galleries are clear and the academy's people can work again, bring it back here and the seal reads READY, and this desk pays you the sixty copper. Nobody at the cleft pays you—their warden confirms the work, we pay the reward. That's the whole arrangement."

She slid it across the counter and was already reaching for the next paper in her stack.

"Read the conditions on the back before you commit to anything past the culling. And don't pry at the deep crystal. The academy gets sour about that."

messages.mes:
The back of the slip carried five printed lines: the cull ran to level one only; the deep galleries past the second gate were academy ground; crystal chipped, broken or pocketed beyond the marked line forfeited the reward and the Guild listing with it. He folded it away with the plate.

Glassmere's north quarter smelled of tallow and wet cobbles. The gate guard glanced at the staff across his back and waved him through without a word, and then the city was behind him and the road ran white and rutted between hedgerows, climbing gently toward a line of grey hills. Carts passed him going the other way, loaded with hay. A boy drove geese off the verge with a switch. Nobody looked twice.

An hour on, the road followed a stream that ran fast and clear out of the hills, and the air off the water had a cold edge to it, the kind that comes off stone in summer. The valley narrowed. The hedgerows gave up and the hills closed in on both sides, and where the stream spilled from the rock the whole hillside had been split like a loaf—a cleft thirty feet across, shadowed inside, and deep in that shadow something caught the light and threw it back in hard little sparks. Glitter, before one was inside.

A path had been worn to the mouth of it. Near the foot of the path stood a plank notice nailed to a post, and beside it a rough shelter of boards and oilcloth, crates of cut crystal stacked under canvas, and a man on a stool with a bill-hook across his knees and a lean yellow dog at his feet.

The dog lifted its head. The man stood, unhurried, and hooked the bill under one arm.

"Hold up there." His voice was flat, used to being obeyed. "This is academy ground. State your business at the cleft."

The watchman took the slip without asking, held it at arm's length, and turned it over once. The stamped seal caught what light there was and gave it back with that same faint shimmer.

"Guild work, then." He handed it back. "Daily's a fair word for it. Beetles come back with the Dungeon's turn like weeds after rain."

The dog came up and sniffed at Alaric's boot, then sat, watching the staff rather than the man.

"Things to know." He counted them off with one thick finger. "First, there's a fee. Ten copper to walk in—the academy's take, not mine. You pay me, I mark you down, in you go. Second, the outer galleries are yours to cull. Past the second gate is academy ground, and I'll know if you've been prying at the deep crystal, because I'm the one who checks what comes out. Third—" he nodded at the crates under the canvas—"the harvesters work the near galleries some days. None are in today, but if you hear picks, it's them, not beetles. Shout before you loose anything at a sound in the dark."

He looked Alaric over once, the staff and the light robes, the same flat assessment he'd give a mule at market.

"Beetles gnaw the crystal and slimes drink the runoff. Slimes are slow and stupid. Beetles are faster than they look and they shatter sharp when they break—keep your eyes out of the spray." He shifted the bill-hook under his arm. "That's the whole of it. Ten copper gets you the gate."

messages.mes:
Alaric counted out the copper into the watchman's broad palm. The man tipped them into a pouch on his belt, licked a stub of pencil, and made a mark in a cheap ledger that lived on a nail under the shelter's eave.

"Loot." He said the word around the pencil. "Beetle shell and slime-leavings, whatever you can carry out—that's yours, Guild custom and mine both. The crystal's another matter." He nodded at the crates under the oilcloth. "Loose chips from the outer galleries, the harvest stakes mark what's the academy's. Anything at a stake or a marked cluster is ours, and I check packs at the gate coming out. Anything else—shards lying free, a shed carapace glittering with it—that's yours to sell, and good luck to you."

He flipped the ledger shut.

"Watch your footing past the first bend. The floor's slick where the stream finds its way in."

The dog yawned, laid its chin back on its paws, and watched Alaric with one eye.

The cleft mouth breathed cool air out at him, faintly mineral, like a cellar. Inside, the daylight reached only a few strides before the walls took over the work: pale crystal veins ran through the rock in slow braided ribbons, and they caught the grey light from behind him and carried it deeper, so the dark ahead was not quite dark—it glittered, softly, the whole way in. The sound of the stream thinned as the path rose above it, and somewhere ahead, faint but unmistakable, came a dry scraping, like a chisel worked patiently at stone.

messages.mes:
The copper changed hands, the pencil scratched its mark, and the watchman tipped his chin at the cleft without another word. The dog's tail thumped once against the boards.

Inside, the light changed the way candlelight does when a door closes. The crystal veins in the walls did the work instead: pale ribbons of it threading the rock, brightening as the daylight behind him thinned, until the gallery ahead glowed faintly with its own cold glitter. The air was cellar-cool and tasted of wet stone. Under his boots the floor was sound rock for the first stretch, then dark with damp where a thread of stream water ran along a channel cut into the floor and slid away into a crack in the wall.

The scraping sound grew as he went. Not one chisel now—several, or one worked fast, a patient grating somewhere around the first bend. Old tracks showed in the wet floor: shallow three-toed gouges, dragged tail-marks between them, leading the same way he was walking. A shed carapace lay against the wall, thumb-sized, translucent, glinting green where the crystal light caught it.

The bend opened into a wider gallery, and there they were.

Two beetles the size of dogs crouched over a low crystal cluster near the far wall, mandibles working at it with that same chisel-grate. Their shells caught the vein-light and threw it back in shards—glassy, faceted, hard to look away from. The nearer one's head came up at the sound of his boots. It turned, antennae tasting the air, and the second one lifted its own head a breath later, still chewing.

The staff came up and the lance went out from where he stood—a spear of flame that crossed the gallery in a blink and struck the nearer beetle full on the shell.

The crack of it filled the gallery. Crystal light scattered wild off the struck shell, and the beetle rocked sideways, legs scrabbling on wet stone, a hiss of seared chitin rising off its back where the plates had gone black and split. It did not die. It screamed instead—a dry, rasping shriek like a file dragged across glass—and came on.

Fast. Faster than something that shape had any right to move. It crossed half the gallery in a scuttling rush, mandibles spread wide, and drove itself up at him before the heat of the spell had faded from the air. The bite caught him across the forearm and forearm-guard, a pincer-crush of pressure and a hot line of pain where the mandible raked through, and then it was shoving its weight against him, shell scraping cloth, legs hooked for grip.

Behind it, across the gallery, the second beetle had abandoned the crystal cluster entirely. It stood with its head high, antennae wide, watching the fight—and watching him.

The wounded one dug in against his side, mandibles working at his arm again, its split shell hissing faintly where the flame had cooked it.
